analysis.one_liner: Strips legal immunity from dominant social media platforms that moderate content by viewpoint or amplify posts users never asked for.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: two Republican senators introduced it, it picked up no additional cosponsors, and it died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend Section 230 of the Communications Act, the law that shields websites from being sued over what their users post. Large platforms would lose that shield if they moderate content in a way that appears to promote or suppress a viewpoint — including demonetizing a creator — or if their algorithms push content at users who never asked for it. Platforms would keep the shield only when restricting material on a specific list of harmful or unlawful grounds, such as obscenity, harassment, violence, or unlawful content, based on an objectively reasonable belief. It would also add a religious-liberty exception, require large platforms to publicly disclose how they moderate content, and make the liability shield something a platform must affirmatively prove in court rather than a protection it automatically enjoys.
analysis.who_benefits: The bill's stated beneficiaries are users who believe a large platform suppressed their speech and online creators whose reach or revenue is cut by platform moderation decisions — they would gain the ability to sue dominant platforms that would otherwise be immune under Section 230. Small businesses and entrepreneurs that build on top of large platforms would gain from a new requirement that platforms publicly disclose their moderation rules and practices. Politically, the bill aligned with conservatives who argue large platforms suppress right-leaning speech, so its more realistic beneficiaries in litigation would be anyone with the resources to sue a dominant platform over moderation decisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users and creators claiming viewpoint censorship

how_it_helps.text: For dominant platforms, Section 230 protection would become an affirmative defense the platform must prove, rather than an automatic shield — so a user claiming viewpoint discrimination could actually get their case before a judge.
Providers would have to publicly disclose their content moderation rules and practices in a form usable by consumers and by entrepreneurs and small businesses building on the service.

The list of reasons a platform may restrict material without losing protection is made explicit — obscenity, harassment, violence, terrorism, self-harm, and unlawful content — replacing the open-ended 'otherwise objectionable' standard with an 'objectively reasonable belief' requirement.

analysis.who_pays: Dominant social media platforms would bear the cost: they would face lawsuits over moderation and recommendation-algorithm decisions they currently cannot be sued over, and they would have to build and publish detailed disclosures of their moderation practices. Ordinary users would also bear indirect costs — platforms facing liability for viewpoint-based moderation could respond by removing more borderline content, leaving spam and harassment up because deleting it carries legal risk, or shutting down recommendation algorithms entirely, all of which change what people see and experience online.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large platforms, and indirectly all users

drawbacks.text: The bill removes liability protection from dominant platforms whenever their moderation 'reasonably appears' to promote or suppress a viewpoint, and whenever their algorithms push content users did not request. That standard is broad enough to invite constant litigation over ordinary editorial and ranking decisions, which platforms could respond to by removing more borderline speech or abandoning recommendations altogether.

By narrowing the 'otherwise objectionable' catch-all to a fixed list and adding an 'objectively reasonable belief' standard, the bill makes it riskier for platforms to remove spam, harassment, and other unwanted material, which could leave users facing more of it.

Making Section 230 protection an affirmative defense means the platform, not the plaintiff, bears the burden of proving it qualifies — a procedural change that would increase the cost of defending even routine cases, a cost likely passed to users through tighter rules or worse service.
The religious-liberty exception would open moderation of religious content to lawsuits under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act standard, creating a new category of legally privileged speech.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer-facing pieces — public disclosure of moderation rules and a clearer list of what platforms may restrict — are modest but real, and the affirmative-defense framing addresses a genuine criticism that Section 230 is applied inconsistently. But the core trade is a steep one: ending immunity for dominant platforms whenever their moderation "appears" viewpoint-based, and whenever their recommendation algorithms push unrequested content, would make running a large open platform far more legally risky. The likely responses — off-platform deaths being more strictly removed, junk content left up because leaving it alone is safer than algorithmic curation, and constant litigation — fall on ordinary users. The bill never received a hearing, so there is no record of how these design problems might have been addressed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in June 2021, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 24, 2021 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote.
The bill never attracted cosponsors beyond its original two Republican sponsors, leaving it with essentially no coalition to push it through committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dominant social media platforms are better off: their Section 230 liability shield remains fully intact and unconditioned, and they face no new disclosure requirements. Users who wanted a legal remedy for alleged viewpoint-based censorship gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the DISCOURSE Act to condition Section 230 immunity on content moderation practices.

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral for the remainder of the Congress, with no hearing, markup, or vote on the record.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans; the bill attracted no Democratic support and died in a committee that took no action on it during the 117th Congress.

industries.industry: Large social media and internet platforms
industries.note: Dominant platforms would lose Section 230 immunity for viewpoint-based moderation, unrequested algorithmic amplification, and hands-on content development, and would face new public disclosure duties. Losing the liability shield is the bill's central threat to their business model, which depends on hosting enormous volumes of user content without publisher liability.

industries.industry: Online content creators and small businesses that depend on platforms
industries.note: The disclosure requirement is written to let entrepreneurs and small businesses understand the rules of the services they build on, and creators who believe their reach or revenue was throttled would gain a legal path to challenge it.

industries.industry: Online users and the broader information ecosystem
industries.note: Users alleging censorship would gain standing to sue dominant platforms, but the same loss of immunity could push platforms toward heavier-handed or more cautious moderation, affecting what everyone sees online.
